15 16 --- 17 18 **Documentation**: [https://www.starlette.io/](https://www.starlette.io/) 19 20 --- 21 22 # Starlette 23 24 Starlette is a lightweight [ASGI][asgi] framework/toolkit, 25 which is ideal for building async web services in Python. 26 27 It is production-ready, and gives you the following: 28 29 * A lightweight, low-complexity HTTP web framework. 30 * WebSocket support. 31 * In-process background tasks. 32 * Startup and shutdown events. 33 * Test client built on `requests`. 34 * CORS, GZip, Static Files, Streaming responses. 35 * Session and Cookie support. 36 * 100% test coverage. 37 * 100% type annotated codebase. 38 * Few hard dependencies. 39 * Compatible with `asyncio` and `trio` backends. 40 * Great overall performance [against independant benchmarks][techempower]. 41 42 ## Requirements 43 44 Python 3.6+ 45 46 ## Installation 47 48 ```shell 49 $ pip3 install starlette 50 ``` 51 52 You'll also want to install an ASGI server, such as [uvicorn](http://www.uvicorn.org/), [daphne](https://github.com/django/daphne/), or [hypercorn](https://pgjones.gitlab.io/hypercorn/). 53 54 ```shell 55 $ pip3 install uvicorn 56 ``` 57 58 ## Example 59 60 **example.py**: 61 62 ```python 63 from starlette.applications import Starlette 64 from starlette.responses import JSONResponse 65 from starlette.routing import Route 66 67 68 async def homepage(request): 69 return JSONResponse({'hello': 'world'}) 70 71 routes = [ 72 Route("/", endpoint=homepage) 73 ] 74 75 app = Starlette(debug=True, routes=routes) 76 ``` 77 78 Then run the application using Uvicorn: 79 80 ```shell 81 $ uvicorn example:app 82 ``` 83 84 For a more complete example, see [encode/starlette-example](https://github.com/encode/starlette-example). 85 86 ## Dependencies 87 88 Starlette only requires `anyio`, and the following are optional: 89 90 * [`requests`][requests] - Required if you want to use the `TestClient`. 91 * [`jinja2`][jinja2] - Required if you want to use `Jinja2Templates`. 92 * [`python-multipart`][python-multipart] - Required if you want to support form parsing, with `request.form()`. 93 * [`itsdangerous`][itsdangerous] - Required for `SessionMiddleware` support. 94 * [`pyyaml`][pyyaml] - Required for `SchemaGenerator` support. 95 96 You can install all of these with `pip3 install starlette[full]`. 97 98 ## Framework or Toolkit 99 100 Starlette is designed to be used either as a complete framework, or as 101 an ASGI toolkit. You can use any of its components independently. 102 103 ```python 104 from starlette.responses import PlainTextResponse 105 106 107 async def app(scope, receive, send): 108 assert scope['type'] == 'http' 109 response = PlainTextResponse('Hello, world!') 110 await response(scope, receive, send) 111 ``` 112 113 Run the `app` application in `example.py`: 114 115 ```shell 116 $ uvicorn example:app 117 INFO: Started server process [11509] 118 INFO: Uvicorn running on http://127.0.0.1:8000 (Press CTRL+C to quit) 119 ``` 120 121 Run uvicorn with `--reload` to enable auto-reloading on code changes. 122 123 ## Modularity 124 125 The modularity that Starlette is designed on promotes building re-usable 126 components that can be shared between any ASGI framework. This should enable 127 an ecosystem of shared middleware and mountable applications. 128 129 The clean API separation also means it's easier to understand each component 130 in isolation. 131 132 --- 133 134

   115	    $ ecs scale --help
   116	    $ ecs run --help
   117	
   118	Examples
   119	--------
   120	All examples assume, that authentication has already been configured.
   121	
   122	Deployment
   123	----------
   124	
   125	Simple Redeploy
   126	===============
   127	To redeploy a service without any modifications, but pulling the most recent image versions, run the follwing command.
   128	This will duplicate the current task definition and cause the service to redeploy all running tasks.::
   129	
   130	    $ ecs deploy my-cluster my-service
   131	
   132	
   133	Deploy a new tag
   134	================
   135	To change the tag for **all** images in **all** containers in the task definition, run the following command::
   136	
   137	    $ ecs deploy my-cluster my-service -t 1.2.3
   138	
   139	
   140	Deploy a new image
   141	==================
   142	To change the image of a specific container, run the following command::
   143	
   144	    $ ecs deploy my-cluster my-service --image webserver nginx:1.11.8
   145	
   146	This will modify the **webserver** container only and change its image to "nginx:1.11.8".
   147	
   148	
   149	Deploy several new images
   150	=========================
   151	The `-i` or `--image` option can also be passed several times::
   152	
   153	    $ ecs deploy my-cluster my-service -i webserver nginx:1.9 -i application my-app:1.2.3
   154	
   155	This will change the **webserver**'s container image to "nginx:1.9" and the **application**'s image to "my-app:1.2.3".
   156	
   157	Deploy a custom task definition
   158	===============================
   159	To deploy any task definition (independent of which is currently used in the service), you can use the ``--task`` parameter. The value can be:
   160	
   161	A fully qualified task ARN::
   162	
   163	    $ ecs deploy my-cluster my-service --task arn:aws:ecs:eu-central-1:123456789012:task-definition/my-task:20
   164	
   165	A task family name with revision::
   166	
   167	    $ ecs deploy my-cluster my-service --task my-task:20
   168	
   169	Or just a task family name. It this case, the most recent revision is used::
   170	
   171	    $ ecs deploy my-cluster my-service --task my-task
   172	
   173	.. important::
   174	   ``ecs`` will still create a new task definition, which then is used in the service.
   175	   This is done, to retain consistent behaviour and to ensure the ECS agent e.g. pulls all images.
   176	   But the newly created task definition will be based on the given task, not the currently used task.
   177	
   178	
   179	Set an environment variable
   180	===========================
   181	To add a new or adjust an existing environment variable of a specific container, run the following command::
   182	
   183	    $ ecs deploy my-cluster my-service -e webserver SOME_VARIABLE SOME_VALUE
   184	
   185	This will modify the **webserver** container definition and add or overwrite the environment variable `SOME_VARIABLE` with the value "SOME_VALUE". This way you can add new or adjust already existing environment variables.
   186	
   187	
   188	Adjust multiple environment variables
   189	=====================================
   190	You can add or change multiple environment variables at once, by adding the `-e` (or `--env`) options several times::
   191	
   192	    $ ecs deploy my-cluster my-service -e webserver SOME_VARIABLE SOME_VALUE -e webserver OTHER_VARIABLE OTHER_VALUE -e app APP_VARIABLE APP_VALUE
   193	
   194	This will modify the definition **of two containers**.
   195	The **webserver**'s environment variable `SOME_VARIABLE` will be set to "SOME_VALUE" and the variable `OTHER_VARIABLE` to "OTHER_VALUE".
   196	The **app**'s environment variable `APP_VARIABLE` will be set to "APP_VALUE".
   197	
   198	
   199	Set environment variables exclusively, remove all other pre-existing environment variables
   200	==========================================================================================
   201	To reset all existing environment variables of a task definition, use the flag ``--exclusive-env`` ::
   202	
   203	    $ ecs deploy my-cluster my-service -e webserver SOME_VARIABLE SOME_VALUE --exclusive-env
   204	
   205	This will remove **all other** existing environment variables of **all containers** of the task definition, except for the variable `SOME_VARIABLE` with the value "SOME_VALUE" in the webserver container.
   206	
   207	
   208	Set a secret environment variable from the AWS Parameter Store
   209	==============================================================
   210	
   211	.. important::
   212	    This option was introduced by AWS in ECS Agent v1.22.0. Make sure your ECS agent version is >= 1.22.0 or else your task will not deploy.
   213	
   214	To add a new or adjust an existing secret of a specific container, run the following command::
   215	
   216	    $ ecs deploy my-cluster my-service -s webserver SOME_SECRET KEY_OF_SECRET_IN_PARAMETER_STORE
   217	
   218	You can also specify the full arn of the parameter::
   219	
   220	    $ ecs deploy my-cluster my-service -s webserver SOME_SECRET arn:aws:ssm:<aws region>:<aws account id>:parameter/KEY_OF_SECRET_IN_PARAMETER_STORE
   221	
   222	This will modify the **webserver** container definition and add or overwrite the environment variable `SOME_SECRET` with the value of the `KEY_OF_SECRET_IN_PARAMETER_STORE` in the AWS Parameter Store of the AWS Systems Manager.
   223	
   224	
   225	Set secrets exclusively, remove all other pre-existing secret environment variables
   226	===================================================================================
   227	To reset all existing secrets (secret environment variables) of a task definition, use the flag ``--exclusive-secrets`` ::
   228	
   229	    $ ecs deploy my-cluster my-service -s webserver NEW_SECRET KEY_OF_SECRET_IN_PARAMETER_STORE --exclusive-secret
   230	
   231	This will remove **all other** existing secret environment variables of **all containers** of the task definition, except for the new secret variable `NEW_SECRET` with the value coming from the AWS Parameter Store with the name "KEY_OF_SECRET_IN_PARAMETER_STORE" in the webserver container.
   232	
   233	Modify a command
   234	================
   235	To change the command of a specific container, run the following command::
   236	
   237	    $ ecs deploy my-cluster my-service --command webserver "nginx"
   238	
   239	This will modify the **webserver** container and change its command to "nginx". If you have 
   240	a command that requries arugments as well, then you can simply specify it like this as you would normally do:
   241	
   242	    $ ecs deploy my-cluster my-service --command webserver "ngnix -c /etc/ngnix/ngnix.conf"
   243	
   244	This works fine as long as any of the arguments do not contain any spaces. In case arguments to the
   245	command itself contain spaces, then you can use the JSON format:
   246	
   247	$ ecs deploy my-cluster my-service --command webserver '["sh", "-c", "while true; do echo Time files like an arrow $(date); sleep 1; done;"]'
   248	
   249	More about this can be looked up in documentation.
   250	https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/task_definition_parameters.html#container_definitions
   251	
   252	
   253	
   254	
   255	Set a task role
   256	===============
   257	To change or set the role, the service's task should run as, use the following command::
   258	
   259	    $ ecs deploy my-cluster my-service -r arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/MySpecialEcsTaskRole
   260	
   261	This will set the task role to "MySpecialEcsTaskRole".
   262	
   263	Ignore capacity issues
   264	======================
   265	If your cluster is undersized or the service's deployment options are not optimally set, the cluster
   266	might be incapable to run blue-green-deployments. In this case, you might see errors like these:
   267	
   268	    ERROR: (service my-service) was unable to place a task because no container instance met all of
   269	    its requirements. The closest matching (container-instance 123456-1234-1234-1234-1234567890) is
   270	    already using a port required by your task. For more information, see the Troubleshooting
   271	    section of the Amazon ECS Developer Guide.
   272	
   273	There might also be warnings about insufficient memory or CPU.
   274	
   275	To ignore these warnings, you can run the deployment with the flag ``--ignore-warnings``::
   276	
   277	    $ ecs deploy my-cluster my-service --ignore-warnings
   278	
   279	In that case, the warning is printed, but the script continues and waits for a successful
   280	deployment until it times out.
   281	
   282	Deployment timeout
   283	==================
   284	The deploy and scale actions allow defining a timeout (in seconds) via the ``--timeout`` parameter.
   285	This instructs ecs-deploy to wait for ECS to finish the deployment for the given number of seconds.
   286	
   287	To run a deployment without waiting for the successful or failed result at all, set ``--timeout`` to the value of ``-1``.
   288	
   289	Scaling
   290	-------
   291	
   292	Scale a service
   293	===============
   294	To change the number of running tasks and scale a service up and down, run this command::
   295	
   296	    $ ecs scale my-cluster my-service 4
   297	
   298	
   299	Running a Task
   300	--------------
   301	
   302	Run a one-off task
   303	==================
   304	To run a one-off task, based on an existing task-definition, run this command::
   305	
   306	    $ ecs run my-cluster my-task
   307	
   308	You can define just the task family (e.g. ``my-task``) or you can run a specific revision of the task-definition (e.g.
   309	``my-task:123``). And optionally you can add or adjust environment variables like this::
   310	
   311	    $ ecs run my-cluster my-task:123 -e my-container MY_VARIABLE "my value"
   312	
   313	
   314	Run a task with a custom command
   315	================================
   316	
   317	You can override the command definition via option ``-c`` or ``--command`` followed by the container name and the
   318	command in a natural syntax, e.g. no conversion to comma-separation required::
   319	
   320	    $ ecs run my-cluster my-task -c my-container "python some-script.py param1 param2"
   321	
   322	The JSON syntax explained above regarding modifying a command is also applicable here.
   323	
   324	
   325	Run a task in a Fargate Cluster
   326	===============================
   327	
   328	If you want to run a one-off task in a Fargate cluster, additional configuration is required, to instruct AWS e.g. which
   329	subnets or security groups to use. The required parameters for this are:
   330	
   331	- launchtype
   332	- securitygroup
   333	- subnet
   334	- public-ip
   335	
   336	Example::
   337	
   338	    $ ecs run my-fargate-cluster my-task --launchtype=FARGATE --securitygroup sg-01234567890123456 --subnet subnet-01234567890123456 --public-ip
   339	
   340	You can pass multiple ``subnet`` as well as multiple ``securitygroup`` values. the ``public-ip`` flag determines, if the task receives a public IP address or not.
   341	Please see ``ecs run --help`` for more details.
   342	
   343	
   344	Monitoring
   345	----------
   346	With ECS deploy you can track your deployments automatically. Currently only New Relic is supported:
   347	
   348	New Relic
   349	=========
   350	To record a deployment in New Relic, you can provide the the API Key (**Attention**: this is a specific REST API Key, not the license key) and the application id in two ways:
   351	
   352	Via cli options::
   353	
   354	    $ ecs deploy my-cluster my-service --newrelic-apikey ABCDEFGHIJKLMN --newrelic-appid 1234567890
   355	
   356	Or implicitly via environment variables ``NEW_RELIC_API_KEY`` and ``NEW_RELIC_APP_ID`` ::
   357	
   358	    $ export NEW_RELIC_API_KEY=ABCDEFGHIJKLMN
   359	    $ export NEW_RELIC_APP_ID=1234567890
   360	    $ ecs deploy my-cluster my-service
   361	
   362	Optionally you can provide an additional comment to the deployment via ``--comment "New feature X"`` and the name of the user who deployed with ``--user john.doe``
   363	
   364	
   365	Troubleshooting
   366	---------------
   367	If the service configuration in ECS is not optimally set, you might be seeing
   368	timeout or other errors during the deployment.
   369	
   370	Timeout
   371	=======
   372	The timeout error means, that AWS ECS takes longer for the full deployment cycle then ecs-deploy is told to wait. The deployment itself still might finish successfully, if there are no other problems with the deployed containers.
   373	
   374	You can increase the time (in seconds) to wait for finishing the deployment via the ``--timeout`` parameter. This time includes the full cycle of stopping all old containers and (re)starting all new containers. Different stacks require different timeout values, the default is 300 seconds.
   375	
   376	The overall deployment time depends on different things:
   377	
   378	- the type of the application. For example node.js containers tend to take a long time to get stopped. But nginx containers tend to stop immediately, etc.
   379	- are old and new containers able to run in parallel (e.g. using dynamic ports)?
   380	- the deployment options and strategy (Maximum percent > 100)?
   381	- the desired count of running tasks, compared to
   382	- the number of ECS instances in the cluster
   383	
   384
